purpose: The citation registry. Every intelligence signal, brief item and knowledge article in the demo seed cites an entry here by `id`. This file is the ONLY permitted source of external URLs in the seed.
rules: NEVER invent, guess or pattern-match a URL. Every entry below was found by search and then actually fetched; none was reconstructed from a remembered pattern.
The seed may cite ONLY entries whose verification.status is VERIFIED. A TODO_VERIFY entry is research output, not demo content.
DO_NOT_CITE entries are excluded from the seed permanently unless the underlying defect is fixed and the entry is re-verified.
`supports_claims` is the contract: a signal may only make a claim that appears there. If a claim is not listed, the page does not support it and the claim must be softened or dropped.
Re-run verification before every rehearsal. The web rots; a 404 on stage is a demo failure.

verification.method: Independent curl check of every URL: follow redirects, 30s timeout, browser user-agent.
verification.network_caveat: Several Akamai-fronted Australian government origins (industry.gov.au, jobsandskills.gov.au, dfat.gov.au, education.gov.au) are unreachable from the build network: TCP 443 opens but the TLS handshake is silently dropped, for every HTTP version and user-agent tried. A sibling origin (abs.gov.au) verifies normally, and research subagents fetched several of these pages successfully earlier in the session. These are therefore recorded as TODO_VERIFY, NOT as dead links: they must be opened manually in a browser on the demo machine before rehearsal.

unsourced_claims: Any fetch-confirmed page giving Australia-Nigeria two-way trade or investment figures. The DFAT country fact sheets are the natural home for this and the whole dfat.gov.au origin was unreachable; no Austrade page I could load carried bilateral trade numbers.

The DFAT Nigeria country brief content (Australia's High Commission in Abuja plus Honorary Consulate in Lagos, Nigerian economy figures). URL exists per search engines but the origin was unreachable - returned as todo_verify, not asserted.

Any Austrade or DFAT page that mentions Nigerian lithium, Nigerian solid minerals, or an Australia-Nigeria critical-minerals partnership. Austrade's West Africa mining analysis covers Ghana, Cote d'Ivoire and Burkina Faso and names gold, bauxite, iron and manganese - not Nigeria and not lithium.

A live Austrade Nigeria education market profile. The old URL austrade.gov.au/Australian/Education/Countries/NIGERIA now returns HTTP 404, and austrade.gov.au/australian/education/education-data/mip-orbis/nigeria-dashboard 301-redirects to the Education Data and Insights homepage. EDI (education.austrade.gov.au) returns HTTP 200 but is a client-rendered app behind 'Login or register', so no Nigeria student-enrolment or visa-grant numbers are publicly readable from it.

Any number of Nigerian students in Australia, or Nigeria-born population in Australia, from an Austrade or DFAT page I could actually load. (ABS or Home Affairs is the right source family for this - recommend assigning it there.)

The 2012 Australia-Nigeria Memorandum of Understanding and the Australia-Nigeria Trade and Investment Commission (ANTIC) on a page I could fetch. These appeared only in a search-engine summary; the High Commission's own relations.html page is a thin link hub and did not contain them.
Smartraveller (DFAT) Nigeria travel advice - www.smartraveller.gov.au was unreachable from this environment, same failure mode as dfat.gov.au.

Any DFAT/Austrade page covering Nigerian passport renewal in Australia. This is correctly the Nigerian High Commission Canberra's function, not DFAT's; DFAT's Protocol directory entry for that mission is the closest verified proxy and is included.

Any Geoscience Australia page referencing Nigeria specifically. GA's published international critical-minerals cooperation is with the US Geological Survey and the Geological Survey of Canada (the Critical Minerals Mapping Initiative). I found no GA page on Africa or Nigeria geological/minerals cooperation. The Nigeria side of the hero thread must be sourced from a different publisher family (e.g. Nigerian Ministry of Solid Minerals Development, NGSA, or Austrade/DFAT).

A standalone lithium commodity page with its own URL. In AIMR 2025 lithium is an in-page anchor inside a combined 'Lithium, Tantalum and Niobium' section on the commodity-summaries page, not a separate document.

Any Geoscience Australia page on lithium REFINING or processing capacity, plant locations, or downstream capability. GA's remit is the resource base; the refined-lithium export figure in the AIMR 2025 introduction is the closest GA gets. Refinery/processing-capacity claims should be sourced from DISR Office of the Chief Economist (Resources and Energy Quarterly) or Austrade instead.

Any Geoscience Australia page on skills, workforce, training pipelines or skilled migration. This is entirely outside GA's remit — nothing found, and nothing should be attributed to GA on that half of the hero thread.

Any industry.gov.au / Critical Minerals Office page that mentions Nigeria, or Africa, in a critical minerals context. The CMO's named bilateral partnerships are the United States, Canada and the European Union; multilateral memberships are Minerals Security Partnership, IEA Critical Minerals Working Party, Sustainable Critical Minerals Alliance, OECD ERGI, IPEF and the Quad. There is no Nigeria hook in this source family — the Nigeria side of the hero opportunity must be sourced from Austrade/DFAT/Nigerian government material, not from DISR.

A dedicated industry.gov.au page for the 'Critical Minerals Facility'. The Facility is administered by Export Finance Australia (exportfinance.gov.au/criticalminerals, live-verified above); DISR only links out to it. I did not invent a DISR URL for it.

The exact URL for the 'Critical minerals funding and support' page linked from the Critical Minerals Office page. My inferred slug (.../critical-minerals/critical-minerals-funding-and-support) returned NO Wayback snapshot, so I could not confirm it exists and I have deliberately not returned it. The link is real on the CMO page; someone with live access to industry.gov.au should click through and capture the true URL.

A standalone URL for the Resources and Energy Quarterly *lithium chapter* on its own. REQ editions are published as one HTML page per edition (with the lithium chapter as an on-page section) plus a single PDF — there is no per-commodity chapter URL.

Any DISR page giving a specific figure for Australian lithium *refining/processing* capacity (tonnes of hydroxide/carbonate). The REQ lithium chapter I read gives export earnings, demand growth and supply growth, but not domestic processing capacity.

A Home Affairs page stating the number of Nigeria-born people in Australia or the number of Nigerian students in Australia — Home Affairs does not publish country-of-birth population counts on these skilled-migration pages; that belongs to ABS and to Department of Education international student data, which are outside this source family.

A Home Affairs page naming Nigeria specifically in a skilled-migration or student-visa context. Nothing in this source family mentions Nigeria. Where visa-charge concessions are named, they cover Pacific Island, Timor-Leste and ASEAN citizens — Nigeria is not among them. Do not let the demo imply a Nigeria-specific Home Affairs migration concession exists; none was found.

A stable, non-JavaScript HTML page listing the Core Skills Occupation List occupations in full. The list is only browsable through the client-side search widget on the Skilled occupation list page, or via the orphaned core-sol.pdf whose currency I could not confirm.

An occupation on the CSOL specifically named for lithium or battery processing. There is no 'Lithium Processing Engineer' or 'Battery Engineer' occupation. The nearest real CSOL occupations are Chemical Engineer (233111), Materials Engineer (233112) and Mining Engineer excluding Petroleum (233611).

An ABS page or release stating the number of Nigerian students in Australia — ABS does not publish student enrolments by nationality; that data belongs to the Department of Education (international student enrolment data) and the Department of Home Affairs (student visa grants).

An ABS statistic for lithium specifically — Mineral and Petroleum Exploration groups lithium inside an 'All Others' category alongside mineral sands, uranium and diamonds, with no separate line. Any lithium production, reserve or refining figure must come from Geoscience Australia or the Office of the Chief Economist, not ABS.

An ABS narrative page (HTML) that states an Australia-Nigeria bilateral trade value. Country-partner detail exists in the International Trade: Supplementary Information data cubes but I did not confirm a Nigeria line, and no ABS landing page prints one.
A Nigeria-born population figure by Australian state more recent than the 2021 Census — ABS data cube 34090DO002 publishes state-level country-of-birth ERP for Census years only.

An ABS release breaking overseas migration flows down by Nigeria as country of birth — the Overseas Migration release publishes only the top five countries of birth (India, China, UK, Australia, New Zealand).
An ABS 'Characteristics of Recent Migrants' release newer than November 2019 — the ABS still flags the Nov 2019 survey as its latest release for that collection.

A Jobs and Skills Australia study dedicated specifically to the CRITICAL MINERALS or BATTERY MINERALS processing workforce. The Clean Energy Capacity Study / 'The Clean Energy Generation' is the closest JSA equivalent, but it is framed around clean energy and net zero, and I did not see lithium or critical minerals named in the page text I retrieved. If the demo needs an explicitly critical-minerals workforce source, it should come from the Department of Industry, Science and Resources Critical Minerals Strategy 2023-2030 (which has a 'Growing a skilled workforce' chapter) rather than from JSA — that is outside my assigned source family and I did not fetch it.

A shortage RATING for Extractive Metallurgist, Metallurgist or Chemical Engineer that is readable from a static, citable URL. The 2025 shortage ratings live inside a JavaScript data tool and downloadable Excel files on the OSL pages; the proxy returned the tool's loading shell, not the per-occupation rating rows. I therefore cannot honestly state from a fetched page that any specific mineral-processing occupation is rated 'in shortage'. Someone should open the OSL tool or the '2025 Occupation Shortage List - 6 digit ANZSCO and OSCA.xlsx' download in a browser and screenshot the specific rows before the demo asserts this.

Any Jobs and Skills Australia page referencing Nigeria, Nigerian-trained workers, or country-of-origin analysis of the skilled migration intake. JSA publishes occupation-level and industry-level analysis, not source-country breakdowns, on its public pages. Nigeria-specific migration and student numbers will need to come from ABS, the Department of Home Affairs, or the Department of Education.

An OSCA-classification occupation profile for Chemical Engineer. Only the deprecated ANZSCO version was findable and fetchable; the OSCA rollout appears incomplete for this occupation as at September 2026.

An official Nigerian government page (msmd.gov.ng or elsewhere on .gov.ng) that states the lithium value-addition-before-export rule as formal policy text. The rule is only attested via the Minister's remarks reported on the Federal Ministry of Information site (fmino.gov.ng). The ministry's own homepage and its news index do not mention lithium or value addition at all.

A working Nigerian Ministry of Foreign Affairs microsite for the High Commission in Canberra. Search engines still index canberra.foreignaffairs.gov.ng/passports/ and /passports/issuance-renewal/, but both are dead (see notes). Do not use any foreignaffairs.gov.ng URL for the consular storyline.
Any Nigerian consulate or consulate-general in Australia beyond the Canberra High Commission. I found no official page evidencing a separate consular post in Sydney, Melbourne or elsewhere.

An official Nigerian government page giving the number of Nigerian students in Australia, or the size of the Nigerian diaspora in Australia. The NBS elibrary has a 'Population and Migration' category but I did not locate a Nigeria-Australia specific release. This number should be sourced from the Australian side (ABS / Dept of Education).

An official Nigerian government page on Nigeria-Australia bilateral trade or investment specifically. NEPC's site covers agricultural non-oil exports (cocoa, cashew, sesame, shea) and did not mention solid minerals or any Australia relationship, so I dropped it as too weak to cite.

The full text of the Ministry of Solid Minerals Development's seven-point agenda on an official ministry page. It is referenced second-hand but I could not fetch a primary ministry document setting out all seven points.
A working page at portal.minesandsteel.gov.ng (the mining cadastre/licensing portal). It returns HTTP 200 but only with TLS verification disabled - its certificate has expired, same as NGSA.

A working Future Battery Industries CRC page at fbicrc.com.au — the domain 301-redirects to poweringaustralia.com.au, which is a different organisation and does not mention the FBI CRC or Curtin. There is no live FBICRC site to cite.
Any Australian university minerals/metallurgy page that mentions Nigeria, a Nigerian institution, or an Africa-specific training program. None of the nine verified pages does.

A dedicated 'Training and Education' page for the Australian Critical Minerals Research Centre — the /training-education path returned the same content as the centre landing page, so I could not confirm it exists as a distinct page.

A standalone Murdoch University 'Hydrometallurgy Research Group' page under Prof Nikoloski — the group is described in trade press but I could only confirm it as part of the Extractive Metallurgy Hub pages.
Confirmation by fetch that the FBI CRC ceased operations on 30 June 2025 — this appeared only in search-result text I did not verify.

A DFAT page on African scholars and Australian mining short courses (dfat.gov.au/news/news/Pages/african-scholars-praise-mining-study-course-in-australia) — it appeared in search results and would be an excellent bridge between AU minerals training and Africa, but two fetch attempts failed (60s timeout, then ECONNRESET). It is outside my source family anyway; the DFAT researcher should retry it.

An official, fetch-confirmed count of Nigerian students enrolled in Australia. The Department of Education's by-nationality data pages are the correct source but education.gov.au was unreachable from this environment (timeouts / ECONNRESET / curl exit 56), so I could not verify any figure.

An official, fetch-confirmed count of Nigeria-born people resident in Australia. This is ABS census territory and outside what I could confirm here — flag it to whoever holds the statistical-agency remit.

A working Austrade Nigeria education market profile. The widely-cited legacy URL https://www.austrade.gov.au/Australian/Education/Countries/NIGERIA returns HTTP 404, and the replacement Education Data and Insights site (education.austrade.gov.au) resolves but serves no extractable content and is subscription-gated. Do not use the legacy URL — it is dead.

A live Australia-Africa Universities Network (AAUN) page. aaun.edu.au does not resolve in DNS at all, despite still appearing in search results and citing University of Ibadan as a Nigerian member. Treat AAUN as defunct or dormant for demo purposes.

A live UWA Africa Research & Engagement Centre (AfREC) page. afrec.uwa.edu.au does not resolve in DNS. Only a thin UWA Public Policy Institute 'Africa' focus-area page loads, and it names no Nigerian partnership.

A UNSW Nigeria country page. https://www.international.unsw.edu.au/nigeria 302-redirects to the generic international students landing page, so the Nigeria-specific content search engines still index no longer exists.

Fetch-confirmed Monash Migration and Inclusion Centre, Alfred Deakin Institute, or ACU Refugees/Migration Centre pages. All three blocked automated retrieval (monash.edu returned HTTP 403, adi.deakin.edu.au served a CAPTCHA challenge, acu.edu.au returned HTTP 403). These centres are almost certainly real and live in a normal browser, but I will not certify URLs I could not load.

Peer-reviewed Australian research specifically on Nigerian migrants or Nigerian students in Australia that is openly accessible. The most relevant candidates were paywalled or blocked: MDPI Nutrients 10.3390/nu18091327 (HTTP 403), Taylor & Francis 10.1080/07256868.2025.2519225 (HTTP 403), and a Springer chapter on Africa-Australia economic engagement (auth redirect). None are safe to click live on stage.

A public Pilbara Minerals / PLS operations page I could actually load — pls.com and www.pls.com/assets/pilgangoora-operation both returned HTTP 403 Forbidden to WebFetch on every attempt. The pages appear to exist (they surface in search) but I could not confirm their content, so I am not returning them. Do not cite PLS from this research pass.

EPA Western Australia pages (epa.wa.gov.au) for the Albemarle Kemerton Plant and the Covalent Lithium Hydroxide Refinery proposals — returned HTTP 403 Forbidden. These would have been excellent regulator-grade citations for plant capacity; they need a manual browser check.

A jtsi.wa.gov.au page — JTSI content now redirects into wa.gov.au under the Department of Energy and Economic Diversification. I found no live jtsi.wa.gov.au URL worth citing; use the wa.gov.au pages returned instead.

Any Australian lithium refinery page that publicly states it is EXPANDING refinery (not mine/concentrate) capacity and needs processing workers. As of Sept 2026 the WA refinery picture is contraction, not expansion: Albemarle Kemerton is in care and maintenance, and TLEA/IGO Kwinana is impaired with Train 2 suspended. Covalent's Kwinana refinery is ramping up and its MINE is expanding — that is the closest true fit.

Any page from this source family connecting an Australian lithium operator to Nigeria, African recruitment, or an overseas skilled-migration training pipeline. I searched for it and found nothing. That link must be built from Australian migration-policy and Nigerian institutional sources, not asserted from company pages.

A page from ANY publisher stating that an Australian lithium REFINERY (as distinct from a mine or concentrator) is EXPANDING its processing capacity. As at September 2026 no such expansion exists to cite. The verifiable Australian downstream lithium picture is: Covalent's Kwinana refinery ramping up toward its existing 50 ktpa nameplate (the one true positive); Albemarle Kemerton with Train 2 in care and maintenance since July 2024 and, per press reporting I did not certify, Train 1 idled in February 2026; and Tianqi/IGO Kwinana with Phase 2 construction halted since January 2025. The July 2026 Covalent 'expansion' already in the inventory is a MINE and concentrator expansion (spodumene concentrate 380 to 760 ktpa), NOT refinery capacity — the demo must not blur those two.

An Australian lithium refinery operator's own public page stating that its ramp-up is generating demand for processing or metallurgical talent. I fetched Covalent's careers portal (https://careers.covalentlithium.com/) and it loads, but it advertises no open roles, lists no processing or metallurgy positions, and its body text still describes the operation as 'currently under construction' — stale and misleading, so I dropped it. I also fetched the one specific Covalent role that surfaced in search (Process Operator, Kwinana, posted 6 Oct 2025) and it now reads 'Sorry, this position has been filled.' Live job listings rot within weeks and are unsafe for a demo; do not cite SEEK, Indeed or ZipRecruiter listings.

The Australian Government Critical Minerals Strategy 2023-2030 chapter '6. Growing a skilled workforce' (https://www.industry.gov.au/publications/critical-minerals-strategy-2023-2030/our-focus-areas/6-growing-skilled-workforce). Search engine summaries indicate it says the sector 'needs highly skilled metallurgists, mining engineers, industrial chemists, earth scientists' and that a lack of skilled workers is a significant risk, and that Australia will 'consider how to better target and apply skilled migration settings to support industry needs' — which would be the perfect bridge between the lithium half and the migration half of the hero thread. I could NOT verify it: three WebFetch attempts returned 60s timeout / ECONNRESET, and a direct curl with a browser user-agent returned curl exit 28 (timeout, 0 bytes) and exit 56 (connection reset). The whole industry.gov.au origin is unreachable from this environment, the same failure mode the earlier sweep hit on dfat.gov.au and education.gov.au. Someone on a normal connection should open this URL and capture it — it is likely the single highest-value missing citation in the whole registry.

A Jobs and Skills Australia or Home Affairs page giving a 2025/2026 shortage rating specifically for Extractive Metallurgist, Metallurgist or Chemical Engineer. I did not re-attempt this (the earlier sweep established the ratings sit inside a JavaScript tool and Excel downloads), and nothing I found this pass changes that.

A regulator-grade page evidencing refinery capacity or workforce. The EPA WA page https://www.epa.wa.gov.au/proposals/covalent-lithium-hydroxide-refinery-s46-2490 DOES load via curl (HTTP 200, contrary to the earlier sweep's 403) and I read it, but its content is thin and off-point: proponent Covalent Lithium Pty Ltd, proposal description 'Change the implementation conditions relating to greenhouse gas emissions', last updated 25 November 2024. It carries no capacity, production or workforce information, so I did not return it.

A per-occupation shortage RATING for Metallurgist, Extractive Metallurgist or Chemical Engineer published by Jobs and Skills Australia on a page I could load. jobsandskills.gov.au was completely unreachable from this environment for the whole session (curl exit 28 timeout / exit 56 connection reset, and WebFetch timeout/ECONNRESET, including on the bare homepage). I attempted: the 2025 OSL Key Findings Report PDF, the 2025 OSL Methodology PDF, the Metallurgists occupation profile at /data/occupation-and-industry-profiles/occupations/234912-metallurgists, and the Occupation Shortage Report - September 2025 publication page. The Metallurgists profile URL does surface in search results and is very likely live for a normal browser, but I did not load it and am deliberately not returning it.

A live-fetched copy of the Australian Government's own statement of the shortage. The Critical Minerals Strategy 2023-2030 focus area 6 page is exactly right and I verified its full text from an Internet Archive capture dated 11 May 2026, but industry.gov.au was unreachable from this environment across ~6 attempts. It is returned as todo_verify: true, not asserted as fetch-confirmed.

Any current (2024-2026) Australian government or peak-body source stating that CHEMICAL ENGINEERING is in shortage. The evidence I found points the other way: Engineers Australia's August 2024 Labour Market Overview reports Chemical and Materials Engineers with the lowest engineering vacancy share of any group (0.7%, 44 vacancies in June 2024), and chemical engineering is absent from Engineers Australia's November 2025 list of specialisations in shortage. Recommend removing 'chemical' from the demo claim.

Any source stating a shortage of workers specifically in LITHIUM refining, battery-chemical processing or hydroxide/carbonate plant operation. Every shortage source I verified is pitched at mining, resources or critical-minerals level. There is no Australian occupation called 'lithium processing engineer' and no published shortage measure at that granularity.

A static, non-JavaScript page anywhere that prints the WA State Priority Occupation List rating for Metallurgist or any mining occupation. The WA SPOL landing page (verified, wa.gov.au) confirms the 350+ occupation rating system exists and that it feeds the WASMOL, but the ratings themselves are only inside a linked Power BI dashboard. Same structural limitation as the JSA OSL tool.

A shortage or workforce-demand source that names Nigeria, Nigerian-trained engineers, or any Africa-sourced training pipeline. I searched across Engineers Australia, AUSMASA, AusIMM, MCA, CME WA, Migration WA and WA DTWD. Nothing in this source family mentions Nigeria or Africa at all. The Nigeria side of the corridor still has to be built from the Nigerian institutional sources and the Australia Awards material already in the inventory - it cannot be asserted from any Australian shortage document.

A fetch-confirmed AREEA (Australian Resources and Energy Employer Association) Resources and Energy Workforce Forecast 2025-2030. The forecast is real and widely reported, but the only URL I found for it sits under areea.com.au/member-portal/, i.e. behind membership, so I did not attempt to present it as a public citation.

A current CME WA (Chamber of Minerals and Energy of Western Australia) workforce-shortage figure. cmewa.com.au loads fine, but the workforce documents I could surface were a 2018-2028 Resources Sector Outlook and pre-budget submissions; the widely-quoted '40,000 additional workers / 33,000 shortfall' figure traces to a 2021 Pit Crew Consulting report reported in news media, which I did not verify against a CME primary page. Do not use that figure without a primary check.

The International Engineering Alliance's official Washington Accord signatory register (ieagreements.org), which is the authoritative source for COREN's provisional-vs-full status and for confirming Engineers Australia as a signatory. The domain does not resolve in DNS from this environment at all — both www.ieagreements.org and ieagreements.org returned 'Could not resolve host' via WebFetch and via curl. COREN's own .gov.ng press briefing is returned instead as the primary source, but it is the Nigerian side self-reporting. Someone with working DNS should verify the IEA register before the demo.

Any Engineers Australia page stating that COUNTRY-level provisional signatory status (Nigeria's status) excludes an applicant from the Washington Accord pathway and forces the CDR pathway. Engineers Australia's own page states only that a PROGRAM must be 'fully accredited, provisional accreditation isn't sufficient' — that is program-level, not country-level. The country-level claim appears only in commercial migration-agent blogs (visaenvoy, cdraustralia, migratio etc.), which I did not treat as citable. The demo should not assert it.

A fetch-confirmed list of which specific engineering occupations sit on the WA Skilled Migration Occupation List (WASMOL) Schedule 1 or 2 — i.e. whether Chemical Engineer (233111), Materials Engineer (233112), Mining Engineer (233611) or Extractive Metallurgist are WA-nominatable. The lists are only served through a client-side JavaScript filter widget on the Migration WA State Nominated Migration Program page; I probed two plausible standalone WASMOL URLs and both returned HTTP 404, and I refused to guess a third. This needs a manual browser check and screenshot.

A standalone, fetch-confirmed Home Affairs page presenting the full skilled migration POINTS TABLE (the per-factor breakdown: age bands, English level, years of skilled employment, qualifications, partner points). The official points calculator page is verified and returned, but it renders the factors inside a JavaScript form rather than as static readable text, and the only full points tables I found in search results were on third-party migration-agent sites and a squarespace-hosted PDF, none of which are citable. The '65 points minimum' figure IS verified from the subclass 189 points-tested page.

Any Australian Government skilled-migration page — Home Affairs, Migration WA, or Engineers Australia — that mentions Nigeria specifically. Consistent with the earlier sweep's finding, nothing in this source family names Nigeria. The Nigeria half of this claim can only be carried by the Nigerian side (COREN) plus the ABS Nigeria-born population data already in the inventory. The demo must present the pathway as one Nigeria-eligible in the same way it is eligible to any non-exempt country, NOT as a Nigeria-specific arrangement.

Confirmation of the content of the '2025-26 WA SNMP Criteria - July 2025' PDF (https://migration.wa.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-05/2025-26%20WA%20SNMP%20Criteria%20-%20July%202025.pdf). It returns HTTP 200 as a genuine 488KB application/pdf, but no PDF text-extraction tooling was available in this environment (poppler/pdftotext absent, and WebFetch could not parse the binary), so I never saw its content and have deliberately NOT returned it as a citation.

Department of Industry, Science and Resources — Critical Minerals Strategy 2023-2030, chapter '6. Growing a skilled workforce' (https://www.industry.gov.au/publications/critical-minerals-strategy-2023-2030/our-focus-areas/6-growing-skilled-workforce). This surfaced in search and is very likely the single best government-level source for Australian critical-minerals workforce training capability, but industry.gov.au was UNREACHABLE from this environment: two attempts timed out at 60s and a third failed with ECONNRESET — the same failure mode the earlier sweep reported for dfat.gov.au and smartraveller.gov.au. I have deliberately NOT returned the URL as a citation because I could not see its content. Someone with working access should fetch it and capture verbatim text before the demo relies on it.

The canonical national register record for RII30420 Certificate III in Resource Processing at training.gov.au. training.gov.au is a client-rendered single-page application: https://training.gov.au/Training/Details/RII30420 and .../PMA30120 both returned HTTP 200 with an empty body on every fetch attempt, so no qualification text could be read. The companion PDF at https://training.gov.au/TrainingComponentFiles/RII/RII30420_R1.pdf downloaded successfully but is image-based/compressed and yielded no reliable extractable text. Use the Jobs and Skills WA page (returned above) as the citable proxy — it states the same qualification code and description in readable HTML.

Any Australian training institution, TAFE or university page that names Nigeria, a Nigerian institution, or an Africa-specific cohort in a mineral-processing or metallurgy training context. I searched this explicitly ('Australian TAFE university mineral processing metallurgy training program Nigeria African students partnership') and found nothing. This confirms the earlier sweep's finding independently. The Nigeria side of the training corridor must be constructed from Nigerian institutional sources (NIMG Jos) plus Australian migration-policy sources — it cannot be asserted from any Australian training-provider page.

A current (post-2021) national assessment of Australia's vocational training capability for critical-minerals or battery-minerals processing. The MRIWA/South Metropolitan TAFE plan returned above is dated August 2021 and is the most recent such document I could fetch. If the demo needs a current-year figure on processing training capacity, it does not exist in a source I could verify.

A live Future Battery Industries CRC page. Confirmed again this pass: the FBI CRC's own URLs (fbicrc.com.au/...) surface in search but the organisation's site does not serve the report; the only live copy of its vocational skills plan I could retrieve is the MRIWA-hosted PDF. Do not cite any fbicrc.com.au URL.

An official Nigerian federal government (.gov.ng) page that NAMES the Nigeria High Commission in Canberra or any Nigerian post in Australia. I fetched the Ministry of Foreign Affairs missions directory at https://www.foreignaffairs.gov.ng/diplomatic-missions/ — it loads and describes Nigeria's 'vast network of diplomatic missions worldwide' but contains no mention of Australia or Canberra anywhere in its content. So the Australia-specific leg of this claim rests on (a) the mission's own site nigeria-can.org.au and (b) the Australian DFAT Protocol directory entry already in the inventory. That pairing is sound, but there is no Nigeria-sovereign page naming the post.

A live canberra.foreignaffairs.gov.ng site. Re-confirming the earlier sweep's finding with a more precise diagnosis: the host is still indexed by search engines (https://canberra.foreignaffairs.gov.ng/, /passports/, /passports/issuance-renewal/, /officer/) but the TLS certificate served does not cover it — error was 'Host: canberra.foreignaffairs.gov.ng is not in the cert's altnames: DNS:dipid.foreignaffairs.gov.ng, DNS:www.dipid.foreignaffairs.gov.ng'. Any foreignaffairs.gov.ng subdomain URL for the Canberra mission will throw a browser certificate warning on stage. Do not use one.

A usable Nigerians in Diaspora Commission (NIDCOM) page. https://nidcom.gov.ng/ surfaced in search with the page title 'AZTEC88 : Nigerians in Diaspora Commission' — a strong indicator the domain is currently SEO-spam-compromised. I did not fetch it further and it must not be cited or clicked live.

Any evidence of a second Nigerian consular post in Australia (a Consulate or Consulate-General in Sydney, Melbourne, Perth or Brisbane). Consistent with the earlier sweep, everything points to Canberra being Nigeria's sole post in Australia. Search-result text (unverified, from an aggregator not a government source) additionally suggested the Canberra High Commission is concurrently accredited to Fiji and New Zealand — I could NOT confirm that on any official page and it should not be asserted.

A Nigeria Immigration Service page that lists Australia, or the Canberra mission, as a named processing embassy. The NIS passport portal (https://passport.immigration.gov.ng/) resolves with title 'Nigerian Immigration Services | Passport' but is a client-rendered application that returned no extractable content — the processing-embassy dropdown is only visible after starting an application. The NIS appointment tool at appointments.immigration.gov.ng/availability has the same shape. citations.title: Shortages ease but gaps persist in 2025 Occupation Shortage List
citations.summary: JSA's release announcement for the 2025 Occupation Shortage List and the accompanying Occupation Shortage Drivers report. citations.title: 2025 Core Skills Occupations List (CSOL) Consultations
citations.summary: JSA's page on the Core Skills Occupation List, the migration occupation list that underpins the employer-sponsored Skills in Demand (subclass 482) visa. It explains that the CSOL process starts with JSA's Occupation Shortage List, then analyses whether migration is an appropriate path to address the identified shortage — considering migrant labour market outcomes, reliance on sponsored visa holders, the domestic graduate pipeline, and market salary. It states over 800 skilled occupations (Skill Level 1 to 3) were in scope for the 2025 CSOL, that consultations opened 25 August 2025 and JSA submitted its advice to Government on 20 October 2025, and that the Minister for Immigration is the final decision maker. It notes the 2024 Skills in Demand salary thresholds of $141,210 (Specialist Skills Stream) and $76,515 (Core Skills Stream).

JSA assesses the domestic graduate pipeline when deciding whether migration is the appropriate response to a shortage
